Foreword
The Indonesia–United Nations Sustainable Development 
Cooperation Framework (Cooperation Framework, 2026–
2030) represents the collective commitment of the UN system 
to fully align its expertise, resources, and partnerships in 
support of Indonesia’s national development vision. Rooted 
in a shared commitment to the Sustainable Development 
Goals (SDG), it is the primary instrument guiding the strategic 
collaboration between the Government of Indonesia and the 
UN Country Team through to 2030.
The Cooperation Framework is a product of extensive, 
inclusive consultations with government institutions, civil 
society, youth, private sector actors, and development 
partners. It is designed to support accelerate progress toward 
Indonesia’s long-term aspiration of becoming an advanced, 
sustainable, and high-income nation, as articulated in and 
the National Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMN 
2025–2029), particularly the “Trisula Pembangunan” which 
emphasizes poverty reduction, human capital development, 
and economic growth. It shows strong alignment between 
the Cooperation Framework with national priorities, while 
ensuring that no one is left behind.
The Cooperation Framework sets out how the UN will adapt 
its ways of working in response to Indonesia’s dynamic 
development context through an increased focus on unlocking 
innovative financing to scale up SDG impact, leveraging the 
capacities of different entities through integrated offers, 
focusing on themes and regions where needs are greatest, 
and facilitating South-South and Triangular Cooperation.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation 
Framework (Cooperation Framework) reflects the strong 
partnership between the Government of Indonesia and 
the United Nations system. It outlines our joint strategy 
to accelerate Indonesia’s progress towards the national 
development objectives and the Sustainable Development 
Goals (SDGs), guiding the work of all UN entities over the 
coming five years.
The Cooperation Framework was designed through a 
participatory process reflecting the perspectives of a broad 
diversity of stakeholders. High-level consultations with 
the Government of Indonesia, development partners, the 
private sector, and civil society organizations ensured that 
it is responsive to national priorities. Further consultations 
included engagement with young people, women’s 
organizations, organizations of persons with disabilities, 
religious organizations, and trade unions. 
The Cooperation Framework reflects the importance 
of the three longer-term transformations enshrined in 
the National Long-Term Development Plan (Rencana 
Pembangunan Jangka Panjang Nasional, RPJPN1) that 
will make Indonesia’s vision of becoming an advanced, 
sustainable, high-income nation possible: Social 
transformation, essential for human resource development, 
which prioritizes universal healthcare, quality education, 
and adaptive social protection, and aims to reduce poverty 
and malnutrition; Governance transformation, which 
emphasizes accountability and transparency, accompanied 
by strengthening the rule of law and enhanced regional 
equity and autonomy to address disparities; Economic 
transformation, which focuses on sustaining high GDP 
growth, the expansion of Indonesia’s middle class, 
boosting manufacturing and digital solutions, achieving a 
diversified renewable energy mix to support the transition 
towards a green circular economy, and investment in smart 
sustainable cities and infrastructure.
The Cooperation Framework is strategically aligned and 
contributes directly to the ‘Asta Cita’ and national medium 
term development plan (Rencana Pembangunan Jangka 
Menengah Nasional, RPJMN2) and in particular the eight 
quick wins, which places a central emphasis on inclusion,
resilience and sustainability. These core principles are also 
central to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and 
achievement of the SDGs. Inclusion promotes a focus on 
equity and the empowerment of women as well as meeting 
the needs of children and youth, the elderly, and persons 
with disabilities. It seeks to close geographic disparities 
where they occur. Sustainability ensures a balance is 
struck between economic development and preserving 
and conserving Indonesia’s abundant natural resources 
and biodiversity as the foundation for long-term prosperity. 
Resilience fosters investments in institutions, systems 
building, and the necessary anticipatory capabilities 
to endure inevitable periods of disruption and shocks, 
including as a result of climate change and especially 
amongst populations in the most vulnerable situations. 
The Cooperation Framework is structured to support the 
achievement of three outcomes aligned to the long-term 
national transitions, medium-term priorities, and the SDGs. 
The first outcome addresses human development and is 
aligned directly with RPJMN priorities 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7 and the 
social and governance transformations under the RPJPN. 
This outcome includes two focus areas. The first outlines 
UN support for inclusive and equitable systems for human 
resources development. The second focus area relates to 
economic and social inclusion for all, addressing multiple 
disparities, including populations in vulnerable situations. 
Across these, efforts will include working to strengthen the 
climate resilience of national systems.
The second outcome of the Cooperation Framework 
addressing nature, decarbonization, and resilience is 
aligned with national priorities 2, 6 and 8 and the economic 
transformation envisioned under the RPJPN. It focusses on 
strengthening biodiversity conservation and sustainable 
resource management, decarbonization, climate resilience, 
the just energy transition and anticipatory disaster 
management.
The third outcome of the Cooperation Framework supports 
economic and digital transformation, supporting the 
economic and digital transformation and aligning to RPJMN 
priorities 2, 3, 5, 6, 7. It outlines two focus areas. Under the INDONESIA-UN COOPERATION FRAMEWORK 2026-2030 7
first, the UN will provide policy and technical support to 
strengthen, resilience and sustainability of the economic 
transformation in line with key national priorities. Under 
focus area two, the UN will provide support for Indonesia’s 
digital and data transformation in line with national policies 
and aligned with the UN Digital Global Compact to promote 
digital access and narrow digital divides.
For each of the three outcomes the UN will leverage 
its comparative advantage to support the Government 
and contribute to national development priorities by 
working across the inter-connected social, economic, 
and environmental development landscape. It will provide 
system-wide integrated policy support and technical 
assistance, engaging with top international experts, 
grounded in sound data and analytics and best available 
scientific evidence-based approaches, including through 
the use of strategic foresight and modelling. A human 
rights-based approach will be embedded to ensure that no 
one is left behind, particularly focusing on the people living 
in the most vulnerable situations. 
Recognising that financing is a key binding constraint 
across priorities, the UN will step up its engagement as a key 
facilitator for unlocking innovative financing to accelerate 
SDG impact at scale, including strengthening partnerships 
with international financial institutions and philanthropic 
actors to mobilize additional resources for sustainable 
development. The UN will also seek to expand and deepen 
partnerships with the private sector, in particular working 
with the Indonesia Global Compact Network to strengthen 
engagement with the 2030 Agenda.
The UN will engage with national and sub-national 
institutions and local communities to develop targeted, 
context appropriate interventions and to build and 
strengthen capacities that support SDG localization to 
narrow geographic disparities by enhancing local ownership 
and institutional sustainability.
The UN will also play a critical role in facilitating knowledge 
sharing through South-South and Triangular Cooperation to 
ensure development solutions are exchanged across the 
global south. To support this, it will convene platforms that 
facilitate innovation and partnerships for technology driven 
development solutions. Regular monitoring, evaluation, 
and adaptive learning processes will be embedded to track 
progress, ensure effectiveness, and enable evidence-based 
decision-making. These efforts will be complemented by 
strengthened accountability mechanisms and participatory 
approaches to ensure inclusive governance.
Support will be anchored within the principles of the 
universal normative frameworks and conventions to which 
Indonesia is party, whilst leveraging UN global and regional 
assets and capabilities. 
The strategy to effectively deliver across the three outcome 
areas centres on applying the principles of the Funding 
Compact3 to establish a strategic whole-of-UN mechanism 
to direct work in accordance with the agreed focus areas. 
This approach will combine technical capacities and 
financial resources through joint programmes and pooled 
funding mechanisms to comprehensively support national 
priorities, and create a platform for dynamic collaboration 
between Government, development partners, and the UN 
to achieve maximum efficiencies and impact at scale. This 
strategic approach will position the UN to better navigate 
complex transitions and deliver more sustainable and 
impactful development outcomes.
The Cooperation Framework sets the direction for all 
UN entity country programming documents, strategies, 
and projects. Its implementation will be overseen by 
two key mechanisms, both meeting at least annually. 
Strategic coordination will be provided by the IndonesiaUN Consultative Forum (IUNCF), co-convened with the 
Ministry of Foreign Affairs, with participation from the 
Ministry of National Development Planning (BAPPENAS), 
line ministries and the UNCT. This platform facilitates 
leadership dialogue on the strategic direction of 
Cooperation Framework implementation, with a particular 
focus on in-depth thematic discussions to ensure alignment 
with evolving national priorities and global commitments. 
Structured oversight of the results achieved by the UN 
under the Cooperation Framework will be provided by 
the BAPPENAS-UN Forum, co-convened with BAPPENAS 
with participation by line ministries and the UNCT. This 
platform will review implementation progress, indicators, 
and targets, maintaining oversight of the Cooperation 
Framework throughout implementation. 
The Results Framework for the Cooperation Framework 
is based principally on nationally established indicators, 
baselines, and targets, disaggregating data wherever 
possible to identify people in the most vulnerable situations. 
A multi-year funding framework and partnership strategy 
will be developed by the UNCT to provide a structured 
approach to financing and collaboration. This will contribute 
to Indonesia’s Integrated National Financing Framework 
for SDG acceleration, aligning resources with national 
development priorities while leveraging innovative financing 
solutions and multi-stakeholder partnerships.8 INDONESIA-UN COOPERATION FRAMEWORK 2026-2030
1.1 Country Context
Indonesia is a large and diverse nation in pursuit of an 
impressive development trajectory. As an upper middleincome country, Indonesia has significant voice and 
influence on the global stage. It is a central player in the 
Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and a 
member of the G20, reflecting its growing economic and 
political importance. 
Economically, the country has averaged 5 percent growth 
over the past five decades whilst several megatrends are 
propelling Indonesia forward. First, with a population of 
281 million, Indonesia is the world’s fourth most populous 
country4. The second is a young and dynamic population 
expected to peak around 2030, which has the potential 
to yield powerful demographic dividends with supportive 
socio-economic and human capital policies. The third is the 
rise of the middle class, which can continue to further stoke 
and consolidate economic progress. Finally, the forces 
of urbanization contribute to cities becoming engines 
of economic and social transformation projected to be 
home to 70 percent of Indonesians in 2045. In addition, 
the country possesses a rich and diverse endowment of 
natural resources with which to drive progress. Yet, amidst 
these solid foundations for growing prosperity, there are 
divides and disparities that will need to be bridged to secure 
Indonesia’s long-term position for inclusive, resilient and 
sustainable development. 
1.2 National vision for sustainable development
The Government of Indonesia has articulated a clear 
development vision of becoming an advanced and 
sustainable high-income nation, set out in the 20-year 
National Long-Term Development Plan (RPJPN)5. More 
specific priorities for the first phase of the RPJPN are 
articulated in the medium-term 5-year plan, RPJMN6, 
underpinned by the eight missions, 17 priority programmes 
and the eight Quick Wins of ‘Asta Cita’ – which align closely 
with the SDGs. These include ensuring food, energy and 
water security and sustainable growth. 
National vision for sustainable development
The National SDGs Roadmap 2030 articulates Indonesia’s 
level of ambition for SDG achievement, prioritizing targets 
for over 100 SDG indicators. SDG coordination, planning, 
financing, monitoring and reporting mechanisms are 
deeply integrated at national and sub-national levels7. The 
SDGs have been fully costed, with an estimated financing 
gap of 20 percent.8 On climate action, Indonesia requires 
$566 billion of financial investments to achieve its NDC 
targets.9 
Over the course of the 5-year plan, Indonesia aims to 
reduce the national poverty rate to 4.5-5 percent and 
eradicate extreme poverty, increase the Human Capital 
Index to 0.59, and accelerate economic growth of up to 
eight percent. The Eastern region is expected to contribute 
22.4 percent to the national GDP and the country aims to 
reduce GHG emission intensity to 45.17 percent by 2029. 
These targets are designed to ensure sustainable and 
inclusive development, improving the quality of life for all 
Indonesians. 
1.3 Overview of SDGs progress
At least 61.4 percent of Indonesia’s SDG indicators are on 
track (see Figure 2), surpassing the Asia-Pacific average. 
However, whilst national averages provide a compelling

case for overall progress, key human and sustainable 
economic development related SDGs 
require acceleration. The most pressing are SDG 2 (zero 
hunger), SDG 3 (good health and wellbeing), and SDG 7 
(affordable and clean energy).
SDG Progress10
Decades of sustained economic growth has enabled 
Indonesia to secure deep gains in poverty reduction. The 
proportion of people living in extreme poverty stands at 1.5 
percent whilst the population below the national poverty 
line has declined to 9 percent11. Looking ahead, addressing 
inequalities and disparities which are linked primarily to sex 
and geography will be imperative (Figure 2). 
Inequality, reflected in a Gini coefficient of 0.38, manifests in 
disparities across regions, sexes, and socioeconomic groups 
that continue to hinder equitable development. Women earn 
23 percent less than men on average12 and poverty rates are 
slightly higher among women (9.65 percent) than men (9.29 
percent). Persons with disabilities have a poverty rate of 11 
percent, and children with disabilities even more so with a 
poverty rate 17 percent13. Prevalence of poverty is highest 
in peripheral and rural areas, which have experienced lower 
productivity gains.
The Government has already pivoted policymaking to 
address this, classifying 62 out of 514 districts as ‘most 
lagging behind’14 and therefore qualifying for targeted 
development measures. With these efforts, analysis by 
UNESCAP suggests inequalities between population groups 
are narrowing, with access to opportunities improving 
across various population in vulnerable situations. UN 
support provided under this Cooperation Framework will 
strengthen Government’s efforts to further narrow these 
disparities.
Economy
Indonesia’s economic growth, averaging over 5 percent 
annually for the past five decades, has elevated Indonesia to 
upper middle-income country status, with GDP reaching US$ 
1.4 trillion15. Robust domestic consumption, exports, and 
Foreign Direct Investment have driven much of this progress. 
Prudent fiscal management and stable macroeconomic 
policies have provided sound enabling conditions. Exports 
constitute 21 percent of GDP, showcasing Indonesia’s 
growing role in global trade.16
Moving beyond the middle-income status will require 
sustained increases in productivity, and formalization of 
the labour market, where informality remains high at 60 
percent. Moreover, Indonesia’s middle class has seen 
a decline by almost 10 million over the past five years, 
owing attributed to the deleterious economic effects of the 
pandemic, compounded by labour market informality and 
underperformance of the service sector17. 
Against this backdrop, the RPJMN prioritizes economic 
diversification and productivity gains in key sectors, 
including energy, and the sharia, digital, green, and blue 
economies. Increased investments are also proposed 
in infrastructure development, entrepreneurship, the 
strengthening of resilient local value chains and MSME 
ecosystems. Special attention will be paid to industrial 
processing of critical minerals and natural resources. 
The agrifood sector remains vital to the economy, 
accounting for nearly 14 percent of GDP and employing 
nearly half of the population18. One third of Indonesia’s land 
area is utilized for agriculture19, which is integrated within 
a rich diversity of ecosystems and cultures. The majority 
of farmers are over 40 years old20, and the sector depends 
increasingly on unpaid or low-paid women agricultural 
labour21. Progress shows that the proportion of districts 
vulnerable to food insecurity has decreased from 17 percent 
to 13 percent22; however, the agrifood system remains 
susceptible to climate-related hazards. 
Human development
Solid gains have been achieved in critical health outcomes, 
as evidenced by an increase in life expectancy and 10 INDONESIA-UN COOPERATION FRAMEWORK 2026-2030
declines in child and maternal mortality. However, with 189 
maternal deaths per 100,000 live births23, Indonesia has a 
substantially higher Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) than 
its ASEAN neighbours. The Government is determined to 
further lower the MMR as one of its top priority activities 
by investing in primary health care facilities and the health 
workforce, as well as strengthening early detection of risk 
factors. 
Progress has been made in addressing the triple burden of 
malnutrition among children, with reductions in stunting and 
wasting, although stunting is still high by WHO standards 
and rates of obesity across all age groups are a cause for 
concern. Non-communicable diseases account for threequarters of all deaths. There is a high rate of unmet need for 
family planning (11 percent) and discontinuation rate (29 
percent), suggesting the need to improve midwifery skill and 
to ensure equitable access to the sexual and reproductive 
health services. 
Nearly 75 percent of districts and cities are now free of 
malaria.24 However, Indonesia ranks second globally for 
tuberculosis25 and third for leprosy.26 The country witnessed 
28,000 new HIV infections27, with one third women, 
concentrated among higher risk populations, with low 
treatment rates. Mental health issues are also prevalent, 
affecting over one third of young people aged between 10 
and 19 years.28
The percentage of pupils completing secondary education 
has risen and there has been an overall relative increase in 
gross enrolment ratio for tertiary education, contributing 
positively to Indonesia’s Human Capital Index. However, 
learning outcomes remain a concern across all education 
levels. Around a quarter of young people are not in education, 
employment or training, and dropout rates remain relatively 
high. Despite 55 percent of science, technology, engineering, 
and mathematics (STEM) graduates being women, only 
three out of 10 women pursue careers in STEM.29
Social protection systems have been evolving progressively. 
Universal healthcare coverage has reached 98.42 percent 
of the population.30 This transformation has reduced 
financial barriers to healthcare, lowering out-of-pocket 
expenses to 27.5 percent of total expenditure.31 However, 
disparities in access to healthcare services across regions 
and socioeconomic groups persist. A significant portion of 
the population, especially those in the informal economy, 
face limitations in social protection coverage. 
To formalize the informal economy, the Government has 
prioritized extending social welfare coverage with the aim 
of increasing the proportion of informal workers covered by 
the social insurance to 57 percent by 2030. 
Regarding women’s equality and empowerment, female 
labour force participation rates in Indonesia are high by 
comparison to other countries and the share of women 
in professional occupations continues to grow. Women 
entrepreneurs play a crucial role in Indonesia’s economy, 
owning or managing around 64 percent of all MSMEs 
(twice the global average). Their participation is however 
still predominantly in micro enterprises and in the informal, 
sector. Women are also under-represented in positions 
of political and economic leadership and in higher value 
industries, and carry a significant additional burden of 
unpaid care work. Despite progressive legislation, one in 
four women in Indonesia continue to experience physical or 
sexual violence within their lifetime32. 
Indonesia has made significant progress in providing 
access to improved water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) 
as well as reductions in the prevalence of open defecation. 
Almost 94 percent of the population has access to at least 
basic drinking water services, although access to safely 
managed water (around 12 percent) and sanitation (just 
over 7 percent) remains low. A fifth of households do not 
have basic hand washing facilities while 71 percent of 
schools have limited access.
Environment
Despite being ranked among the top ten largest emitters of 
GHG globally and having higher emissions intensities than 
global and regional averages, Indonesia’s CO2 emissions per 
capita are still relatively low. GHG emissions are dominated 
by energy (59 percent) and forestry and other land use 
(FOLU) (18 percent). Emissions are projected to peak by 
2030, then decline steadily to 2050. The country’s NDC 
commitment sets out ambitious plans to reduce emissions 
by between a third and a half by 2030 and achieve net zero 
emissions by 2060. 
Indonesia has significant potential for transitioning to 
diverse and renewable sources of energy. The country is 
committed to achieving a target of a 23 percent renewable 
energy mix. The country is progressing along its energy 
transition, although it is currently utilizing only a fraction 
of its substantial and varied potential. The domestic just 
energy transition has the potential to create 5.86 million 
new green jobs in renewable energy, electric mobility, energy 
efficiency, and resource-efficient manufacturing. INDONESIA-UN COOPERATION FRAMEWORK 2026-2030 11
As a large and diverse archipelago nation, Indonesia is 
one of the most biologically diverse countries in the world, 
providing essential ecosystem services, yet a declining 
Red List Index33 indicates an increasing rate of species 
extinction risk. Despite slightly declining forest, forest areas 
have been increasingly maintained which has positively 
impacted the preservation of critical habitats for biodiversity 
and endangered species. National parks and conservation 
programs have been strengthened by national authorities, 
as part of efforts to balance economic development and 
environmental protection. 
The National Action Plan for Climate Change Adaptation 
aims to strengthen multi-sectoral approaches to climate 
resilience. In this regard, the country is enhancing disaster 
risk reduction, through integration of gender-responsive 
practices/approach, strengthening infrastructure, and 
building community awareness and local response 
strategies in vulnerable regions. 
Financing
Financing for development is supported by a mix of 
domestic and international resources. Government revenue 
remains at approximately 12-13 percent of GDP34, with 
ongoing efforts to enhance tax collection and expand fiscal 
space. Indonesia’s dynamic private sector is attracting 
growing international interest, with foreign direct investment 
reaching $50 billion, primarily from Asian partners such as 
Singapore, China, and Japan.35
Indonesia has emerged as a global leader in innovative 
financing, mobilizing both public and private sector 
investments and leveraging ESG (Environmental, Social, and 
Governance) principles for SDG acceleration, with all limited 
liability companies mandated by law to invest in CSR.36 This 
approach includes accessing capital and carbon markets, 
results-based payments, bonds, Islamic financing, and 
private investments in green and blue economy initiatives. 
Unlocking this market could provide new financing streams, 
while preserving biodiversity, and meeting climate targets.
Official Development Assistance (ODA) plays a niche role, 
complementing domestic resources by bridging funding 
gaps, leveraging impact, piloting innovative approaches, 
and leveraging private sector investment and innovative 
financing. Strategic foresight and international cooperation 
are essential to optimize development financing and ensure 
the alignment of resources with national priorities and the 
SDGs, especially in a global context of declining ODA flows. 
Multidimensional risks
Four inter-connected, multidimensional risks could 
potentially disrupt Indonesia’s pathway to inclusive and 
sustainable development. First, Indonesia is ranked second 
out of 193 countries assessed for disaster risk in the World 
Risk Index by virtue of its location in the Pacific Ring of Fire, 
which is exacerbated by high exposure to climate impacts. 
Second, the country faces risks to population health 
caused by pandemics, zoonotic diseases, environmental 
pollution and the rise of non-communicable diseases. 
Third, cybercrime represents a significant emergent risk, 
with youth and women disproportionately vulnerable and 
impacted, within the context of Indonesia’s ambitious 
digital transformation. Fourth, the country is vulnerable 
to the knock-on effects of fractious global geopolitics, 
conflicts and trade wars, alongside domestic governance 
risks related to ensuring sound standards of integrity, 
transparency, and accountability. Finally, there is a need 
maintain internal social cohesion integral to the national 
goal of strengthening the Pancasila ideology.
Stakeholder Engagement through 
the Cooperation Framework Design
The Cooperation Framework was designed through a 
participatory process allowing perspectives from all key 
stakeholder groups to be reflected, including through 
inputs to the groundwork in the Country Analysis and 
evaluation of the previous Cooperation Framework. Highlevel consultations with the Government of Indonesia, 
development partners, and civil society organizations have 
ensured that the Cooperation Framework is responsive 
to national priorities and emerging needs. Consultations 
also included engagement with young people, women’s 
organizations, migrant workers’ organizations, 
organizations of persons with disabilities, and trade unions. 
The Cooperation Framework benefitted from Voluntary 
National Reviews in 2017, 2019, and 2021, with a further 
review underway for 2025. At the local level, Voluntary 
Local Reviews have been or are being undertaken in at 
least 15 provinces and districts, offering critical data to 
align UN support with national and sub-national priorities.
This is complemented by further, more detailed 
consultations with relevant stakeholder groups by 
individual UN entities as part of the design of their 
respective country plans, which will operationalize the 
overall vision of the Cooperation Framework. This inclusive 
approach ensures that the Cooperation Framework reflects 
diverse perspectives and is aligned with the Government’s 
Asta Cita priorities.12 INDONESIA-UN COOPERATION FRAMEWORK 2026-2030
The Cooperation Framework contributes to the national 
long-term vision and outcomes are designed to directly align 
to the eight priorities of the RPJMN. It is also grounded in 
the core principles of inclusion, resilience and sustainability, 
which are central to the United Nations 2030 Agenda while 
advancing the three core transformations referred above.
The Cooperation Framework is structured to support the 
achievement of three outcomes and five focus areas. The 
first outcome addresses human development and is aligned 
directly with RPJMN priorities 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7 and the social and 
governance transformations under the RPJPN. The second 
outcome covers UN support for nature, decarbonization, 
and resilience and is aligned with national priorities 2 and 
8 and the economic transformation envisioned under the 
RPJPN. The third outcome supports economic and digital 
transformation and aligns to national priorities 2, 3, and 5 
and the economic transformation of the RPJPN. 
UN COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE
At this pivotal stage in Indonesia’s development trajectory, 
the UN will continue to evolve to provide relevant and 
efficient support as the country moves toward high-income 
status.

the Government and contribute to the national development 
priorities by working across the inter-connected social,

The Cooperation Framework is structured around three 
strategic outcomes. It is informed by integrated UN Country 
Analysis and extensive multi-stakeholder consultations, 
which identified the most promising pathways for UN 
engagement in support of sustainable development. 
The Cooperation Framework is strategically aligned to

To deliver effectively across the three Outcomes, the

comprehensively support national priorities, and create a 
platform for effective collaboration between Government, 
development partners, and the UN, through which financial 
resources and technical expertise can be channelled to 
maximum effect and scale.
Specific modalities for this will be defined in dialogue with 
the Government and development partners, potentially 
taking the form of either strategic joint programmes or a 
country-level pooled fund aligned to the three Outcomes 
of the Cooperation Framework. The design will prioritise 
strengthening accountability and transparency of results, 
funding needs, and expenditures.

programmes instead of administrative costs and facilitate 
more integrated ways of working across agencies.
